sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: weight versus weight rating, ball hitch versus fifth wheel, backing a car versus a trailer, loaded versus empty stopping, wide right versus early left turns, plus continuation facts on axle weight, hitch checks, towing awareness, space, rollover ratios and jackknifes
Confusable pairs among the towing rules, followed by continuation facts that did not fit part C; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec10-R01 | anchor: A01
Gross combination weight is what the rig and load actually weigh, while the gross combination weight rating is the maximum combined loaded weight the manufacturer specifies. [A01]
Why it matters: group weight terms; confusable weight versus rating.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-R02 | anchor: A01
Axle weight is the weight one axle or one set of axles puts on the ground. [A01]
Why it matters: group weight terms; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec10-R03 | anchor: A02
A ball-and-hitch coupler joins a ball on the tow vehicle to a coupler on the trailer tongue, whereas a fifth-wheel hitch sits in a truck bed and locks onto a kingpin and is less prone to balance problems. [A02]
Why it matters: group hitches; confusable ball hitch versus fifth wheel.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R04 | anchor: A02
Before towing with a ball hitch, confirm every coupling part is present and unbroken and the trailer tongue is not bent, cracked or damaged. [A02]
Why it matters: group hitches; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R05 | anchor: A02
Flatbed trailers carry a greater risk of the load shifting sideways or falling off, and in bad weather a poorly balanced rig may not stay balanced. [A02]
Why it matters: group loading; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R06 | anchor: A02
Check that the fifth-wheel mounting assembly is solidly attached with no loose or missing parts and that the kingpin is not bent. [A02]
Why it matters: group hitches; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-R07 | anchor: A03
Fifth-wheel electric lines must not be chafed, spliced or worn, the platform supporting the skid plate must be free of cracks, and the release arm must be engaged with any safety latch in place. [A03]
Why it matters: group hitches; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R08 | anchor: A03
Pre-trip, make sure the load is balanced and secured and every outside storage compartment door is latched or locked. [A03]
Why it matters: group inspection; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R09 | anchor: A03
A heavier vehicle makes the brakes work harder and absorb more heat, yet heavy-vehicle brakes, tires, springs and shocks work best when fully loaded. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; confusable loaded versus empty stopping.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R10 | anchor: A03
A lack of awareness is a major cause of crashes, so use your mirrors often, signal, and make other drivers aware of your vehicle even when it is in plain sight. [A03]
Why it matters: group towing safely; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R11 | anchor: A03
Large vehicles take up more space and need more room to stop and turn, so managing the space around a towing rig matters even more than in a car. [A03]
Why it matters: group space; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-R12 | anchor: A04
Backing a car, turn the top of the wheel toward where you want to go; backing a trailer, turn it the opposite way at first and then follow the trailer. [A04]
Why it matters: group backing; confusable car versus trailer backing.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R13 | anchor: A04
While backing a trailer, try to set up a straight-line path, watch the mirrors for drift, and pull forward to reposition whenever needed. [A04]
Why it matters: group backing; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-R14 | anchor: A05
Turning left too early lets off-tracking carry your left side into vehicles beside you, while starting from the inner of two left-turn lanes risks swinging right into drivers you cannot see. [A05]
Why it matters: group turns; confusable early turn versus inside lane.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R15 | anchor: A05
Roads that tilt a vehicle can bring it into signs or trees at the edge, so where that is a risk drive a little closer to the center of the road. [A05]
Why it matters: group clearance; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R16 | anchor: A05
Before backing into an area, get out and look for overhanging trees, branches or electric wires, which are easy to miss while reversing. [A05]
Why it matters: group clearance; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-R17 | anchor: A06
In the rearward amplification chart, a value of 2.0 means the rear trailer is twice as likely to overturn as the truck, and triples reach 3.5. [A06]
Why it matters: group combinations; difficulty high.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-R18 | anchor: A06
Combinations of vehicles are heavier and longer than single vehicles, need more driving skill, and have been involved in many crashes where only the trailer overturned. [A06]
Why it matters: group combinations; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-R19 | anchor: A07
Empty combination rigs take longer to stop than loaded ones because stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction, so allow long following distances and look far ahead to brake early. [A07]
Why it matters: group skids; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-R20 | anchor: A07
A trailer jackknife is more likely when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded; spot it early in the mirrors whenever you brake hard, because once the trailer leaves the lane a jackknife is very hard to stop. [A07]
Why it matters: group skids; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0074]
